whyTempting: It is the one formula every account of this paper quotes, so a reader expects to find it on the page.
whereItIsTrue: The paper's conclusion is the same relation written for a change: a body that gives off the energy \(L\) loses the mass \(L/V^2\), where \(V\) is the speed of light.

whatIsTrue.r0: The paper never writes \(E=mc^2\). It says that a body giving off the energy \(L\) loses the mass \(L/V^2\).
whatIsTrue.r1: The paper states its result on p. 641 as a change: if a body gives off the energy \(L\) as radiation, its mass decreases by \(L/V^2\), with \(V\) the speed of light. It then prints the conversion for everyday units: the mass changes by \(L/9\cdot10^{20}\) when the energy is measured in erg and the mass in grams. It never writes the familiar equation, and it never gives a whole body an energy equal to its mass times the square of the speed of light.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) The letters: \(L\) is the energy the body gives off, and \(V\) is the speed of light. (2) The printed statement: the mass decreases by \(L/V^2\). (3) The printed conversion: \(9\cdot10^{20}\) is the square of \(3\cdot10^{10}\), the speed of light in centimetres per second, so an energy change of \(L\) erg changes the mass by \(L/9\cdot10^{20}\) grams. (4) Worked case: \(L=9\cdot10^{20}\) erg changes the mass by 1 gram. (5) What the page does not contain: an equation giving a body's whole energy as its mass times \(V^2\). The paper works only with differences of energy, and it says its energies carry arbitrary additive constants, so no total energy appears.
whatIsTrue.r3: The familiar equation belongs to later writings, not to this paper. As a relation between changes, the paper's \(L/V^2\) is what later notation writes as \(\Delta m=\Delta E/c^2\).

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 18, 639–641 (1905), plate p. 641
scenario mass-energy-printed-factor: L = 9·10²⁰ erg gives 1 g
